cluster_genes.affinage_functional_annotation: ARF3 is a class I ADP-ribosylation factor (small GTPase) that cycles between GDP-bound inactive and GTP-bound active states on endomembranes, functioning as a master regulator of vesicle coat assembly, cargo sorting, and membrane homeostasis at the trans-Golgi network, recycling endosomes, and the Flemming body during cytokinesis. In its GTP-bound form, ARF3 is recruited to TGN membranes in a BIG1/BIG2-dependent manner—distinct from the broader Golgi distribution of ARF1—where it engages effectors such as GGA1–3 to drive clathrin-coated vesicle formation and mannose 6-phosphate receptor trafficking [PMID:20357002, PMID:10749927]; together with ARF1 it redundantly maintains recycling endosome tubular architecture and transferrin recycling [PMID:22971977]. Beyond canonical trafficking, ARF3 controls macrophage TLR4 inflammatory signaling via BIG1-dependent PI(4,5)P₂ synthesis and TIRAP membrane recruitment [PMID:32415087], modulates NLRP3 inflammasome activation during influenza infection [PMID:40608252], and regulates collective cancer cell invasion through N-cadherin turnover [PMID:36880595]. De novo missense mutations in the ARF3 guanine-nucleotide-binding pocket cause a neurodevelopmental Golgipathy featuring brain malformations, with variants classified as gain- or loss-of-function based on effector binding and Golgi morphology effects validated in Drosophila and zebrafish models [PMID:34346499, PMID:36369169].

cluster_genes.UniProt_functional_annotation: Putative small GTP-binding protein cycling between an inactive GDP-bound and an active GTP-bound form

cluster_genes.affinage_functional_annotation: B3GNT2 is the principal polylactosamine synthase in mammals, catalyzing β1,3-N-acetylglucosamine transfer to extend poly-N-acetyllactosamine chains on N-glycans of diverse cell-surface glycoproteins. Crystal structures in multiple ligand-bound states reveal a sequential kinetic mechanism, with an N-terminal helical domain that contributes to acceptor substrate discrimination and active-site residues whose mutation abolishes catalytic activity [PMID:33158990]. B3gnt2-knockout mice demonstrate dramatically reduced polylactosamine on N-glycans and hyperactivation of T and B cells due to loss of polylactosamine on co-receptors CD28 and CD19, establishing the enzyme as a negative regulator of lymphocyte activation [PMID:20816167]. In cancer, B3GNT2-mediated polylactosamine extension on multiple tumor-surface ligands and receptors disrupts tumor–T cell interactions, conferring resistance to cytotoxic T cell killing, while on the Wnt co-receptor LRP6, polylactosamine extension promotes plasma membrane trafficking and enhances Wnt/β-catenin signalling [PMID:35338135, PMID:36980204].

BLM is an ATP-dependent 3′→5′ RecQ family DNA helicase that functions as the catalytic core of the BTR dissolvasome (BLM–Topoisomerase IIIα–RMI1/BLAP75) to dissolve double Holliday junctions into non-crossover products, thereby suppressing excessive homologous recombination and sister chromatid exchanges [PMID:16595695, PMID:10880455]. Operating as a monomer with ~70–80 bp/s processivity, BLM unwinds diverse substrates including replication forks, G-quadruplexes, R-loops, and telomeric D-loops, with its activity modulated by RPA (which enables reinitiation and bidirectional unwinding at nicks), POT1/TRF2 (at telomeres), and CtIP/DNA2 (during long-range end resection), while RAD51 filaments on DNA block BLM translocation, establishing its anti-recombinase function [PMID:19165145, PMID:32101168, PMID:16030011, PMID:29020620, PMID:31544923, PMID:28912125]. BLM protein levels and activity are tightly cell-cycle-regulated through MIB1-mediated ubiquitination (promoting G1 degradation), TopBP1-dependent stabilization in S phase via phospho-Ser304 recognition, USP37-mediated deubiquitination enhanced by ATM, and AARS1-catalyzed lactylation at Lys24, while phosphorylation by ATM (Thr99), MPS1 (Ser144/PLK1 docking), CDK, and ATR/Chk1 directs BLM to stalled replication forks, DSBs, meiotic synaptonemal complexes, and anaphase ultrafine bridges for sister chromatid decatenation and centromere integrity maintenance [PMID:24239288, PMID:28919440, PMID:34606619, PMID:40634292, PMID:12034743, PMID:16864798, PMID:17599064, PMID:31253795]. BLM additionally participates in rDNA transcription by unwinding GC-rich impediments ahead of RNA Pol I, resolves telomeric R-loops in ALT cells in coordination with FANCM and SLX4IP, and cooperates with p53 at stalled replication forks to regulate recombination and apoptosis [PMID:22106380, PMID:31138795, PMID:31447390, PMID:12606585].

CARNMT1 is a dual-specificity S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methyltransferase that catalyzes histidine Nπ-methylation of both small-molecule dipeptide substrates (carnosine → anserine) and a selective set of C3H zinc finger-containing RNA-binding proteins, including U2AF1, ZC3H15, ZC3H18, RBM22, and RNF113A, at a Cx(F/Y)xH consensus motif [PMID:26001783, PMID:37612136, PMID:40473212]. Protein histidine methylation by CARNMT1 stabilizes zinc finger domain structure, and this modification is functionally required for proper RNA binding by U2AF1, regulation of pre-mRNA alternative splicing, and mRNA degradation mediated by Roquin and TTP [PMID:37612136, PMID:39198440]. Catalytic residues Tyr386, Tyr396, and Tyr398 maintain the reactive conformation during methyl transfer, and CARNMT1 catalytic activity is essential for mouse embryogenesis, as both knockout and catalytically inactive knock-in mice exhibit embryonic lethality [PMID:37612136, PMID:40810683]. The substrate selectivity and enzymatic activity are evolutionarily conserved, with nematode CARNMT methylating homologous C3H zinc finger substrates in vitro [PMID:40473212].

DENR is a specialized translation reinitiation and ribosome recycling factor that functions as an obligate heterodimer with MCTS1 on the 40S ribosomal subunit, where it occupies the eIF1-binding site and evicts residual tRNA from post-termination ribosomes to enable resumed scanning past short upstream open reading frames (uORFs) [PMID:28723557, PMID:30146315, PMID:32938922]. The DENR N-terminal domain coordinates a zinc ion through four conserved cysteines that are essential for MCTS1 heterodimerization, while MCTS1 contributes a tRNA-binding surface required for reinitiation activity [PMID:30584092, PMID:29889857]. Through this uORF-dependent reinitiation mechanism, DENR controls translation of functionally diverse mRNAs including ATF4 during the integrated stress response, CLOCK in circadian rhythm regulation, and JAK2 in interferon–JAK–STAT signaling [PMID:32938922, PMID:30982898, PMID:35440133]. De novo missense mutations in DENR that disrupt its reinitiation activity cause a brain developmental disorder characterized by impaired cortical neuron migration and dendritic morphogenesis [PMID:27239039].

VCF2 is a nuclear cofactor of the AAA-ATPase p97/VCP that directly binds p97 through a novel alpha-helical motif and associates with p97-UFD1-NPL4 and p97-UBXN2B complexes [PMID:37713320]. VCF2 localizes to the nucleus and promotes nuclear import of p97; loss of VCF2 (and its paralog VCF1) reduces nuclear p97 levels, causes slow growth, and confers hypersensitivity to p97 chemical inhibition and DNA damage, establishing VCF2 as a critical regulator of nuclear p97 functions [PMID:37713320].

GTF2B (TFIIB) is a general transcription factor essential for RNA polymerase II preinitiation complex (PIC) assembly, transcription start site selection, promoter clearance, and coupling of initiation to termination. Its C-terminal cyclin-fold core domain recognizes TBP on promoter DNA and contacts flanking BRE elements upstream and downstream of the TATA box, while its N-terminal zinc ribbon domain binds the Pol II dock domain to recruit Pol II–TFIIF; within the PIC, the B-linker assists DNA strand opening and the B-reader positions the template strand for start site selection, with TFIIB displacement triggered by clash with the growing RNA transcript at 12–13 nucleotides to permit elongation [PMID:19820686, PMID:23151482, PMID:9660923, PMID:16230532]. TFIIB is a direct target of diverse transcriptional activators—including acidic (VP16), proline-rich (CTF1), and nuclear receptor classes—whose binding induces conformational changes that modulate TFIIB recruitment and PIC formation [PMID:1922364, PMID:1517211, PMID:10077585, PMID:7583100]. Beyond initiation, TFIIB is phosphorylated at Ser65 within the PIC, linking it to CstF-mediated 3′-end processing, and participates in gene loop formation between promoters and terminators via interaction with the Ssu72 phosphatase, establishing TFIIB as a physical and functional bridge coupling transcription initiation to termination [PMID:20226668, PMID:17803944, PMID:35947745].

HCFC1 (HCF-1) is a large chromatin-associated transcriptional co-regulator that scaffolds opposing histone-modifying complexes to control cell proliferation, cytokinesis, and metabolic gene expression. The HCF-1N subunit, generated by OGT-mediated proteolytic cleavage at HCF-1PRO repeats within the OGT active site, uses its Kelch/β-propeller domain to tether Set1/MLL H3K4 methyltransferase and Sin3-HDAC complexes to sequence-specific transcription factors — including E2F1, THAP11, ZNF143, and VP16 — at thousands of CpG-island promoters, thereby driving G1-to-S progression and context-dependent gene activation or repression [PMID:12670868, PMID:17612494, PMID:23539139]. The HCF-1C subunit ensures proper cytokinesis by regulating PR-Set7 expression and mitotic H4-K20 methylation, and the noncovalently associated subunits are held together by interdigitated Fn3 self-association sequences that also recruit the nuclear localization signal [PMID:12743030, PMID:15200950, PMID:23045687]. Missense mutations in the HCFC1 Kelch domain cause the X-linked cblX disorder through transcriptional failure at the MMACHC promoter, and HCFC1/THAP11 mutations additionally impair ribosome biogenesis gene expression [PMID:24011988, PMID:35013307].

HMGN2 is a nucleosome-binding chromatin architectural protein that modulates higher-order chromatin structure to regulate transcription, replication, and DNA repair. Its 30-amino-acid nucleosome-binding domain contacts two sites per nucleosome core near the dyad axis and entry/exit regions, requiring histone tails for binding and antagonizing linker histone H1 occupancy; incorporation during chromatin assembly unfolds chromatin and enhances RNA polymerase II transcription initiation and DNA replication from nucleosomal templates [PMID:7649479, PMID:9545265, PMID:8107104, PMID:1453455, PMID:28035005]. HMGN2 preferentially associates with acetylated H3 and H2A.Z-containing nucleosomes, maintains active histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K9ac, H3K4me3) at target loci, suppresses H3K27 methylation, and its chromatin binding is negatively regulated by acetylation at K2 (written by PCAF, erased by HDAC6), SUMOylation at K17/K35 (by PIAS1), and succinylation at K30 [PMID:10207070, PMID:41325801, PMID:24872413, PMID:34458839, PMID:27358110]. Beyond its chromatin role, HMGN2 directly interacts with homeodomain transcription factors (PITX2, Lef-1, Dlx2) to inhibit their DNA binding, modulates NF-κB and Nrf2 signaling in innate immune responses, and its alpha-helical domain possesses intrinsic antimicrobial activity against Gram-negative bacteria [PMID:18045789, PMID:35872015, PMID:21518253, PMID:16115376, PMID:31596045].

cluster_genes.UniProt_functional_annotation: Component of the 60-80S U3 small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein (U3 snoRNP). Required for the early cleavages during pre-18S ribosomal RNA processing (PubMed:12655004). Part of the small subunit (SSU) processome, first precursor of the small eukaryotic ribosomal subunit. During the assembly of the SSU processome in the nucleolus, many ribosome biogenesis factors, an RNA chaperone and ribosomal proteins associate with the nascent pre-rRNA and work in concert to generate RNA folding, modifications, rearrangements and cleavage as well as targeted degradation of pre-ribosomal RNA by the RNA exosome (PubMed:34516797)

cluster_genes.affinage_functional_annotation: KDM2A is a JmjC-domain-containing Fe(II)/2-oxoglutarate-dependent histone demethylase that selectively removes mono- and dimethyl marks from H3K36, functioning as a central epigenetic repressor at CpG island-containing promoters and a metabolic sensor that couples nutrient status to rRNA transcription [PMID:25128496, PMID:22083960, PMID:20379134]. KDM2A is recruited to unmethylated CpG islands via its ZF-CXXC domain and engages the nucleosome acidic patch to access H3K36me2, thereby enabling Polycomb (PRC1/H3K27me3)-mediated gene silencing, protecting CpG islands from DNMT3A-catalyzed de novo DNA methylation, and maintaining heterochromatin integrity through HP1 interaction at pericentromeric regions [PMID:36797403, PMID:22083960, PMID:40701999, PMID:19001877]. Beyond histone demethylation, KDM2A functions as an F-box subunit of an SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets β-catenin, TCF/LEF factors, and PFKFB3 for proteasomal degradation, and its chromatin occupancy is dynamically regulated by ATM phosphorylation at T632 during DNA damage, SIRT6-mediated mono-ADP-ribosylation, AMPK-dependent signaling during glucose starvation, and PHF8-mediated inhibition relieved by Ser731 dephosphorylation [PMID:39934243, PMID:37998355, PMID:25823024, PMID:32584788, PMID:26416883, PMID:40427554]. De novo KDM2A variants cause a neurodevelopmental disorder with aberrant DNA methylation profiles, and conditional deletion in male germ cells demonstrates an essential role in meiotic entry through recruitment of E2F1/HCFC1 to meiosis gene promoters [PMID:41468891, PMID:39160277].

KRT16 is a stress-responsive type I keratin that functions both as a structural intermediate filament protein in suprabasal palmoplantar and mucosal epithelia and as a signaling scaffold that modulates innate immunity, cell proliferation, and keratinocyte differentiation. Mutations in the conserved 1A rod-domain helix initiation motif cause focal non-epidermolytic palmoplantar keratoderma [PMID:8595410]. KRT16 is transcriptionally induced by ATF4 during the integrated stress response and by TFAP2A in lung adenocarcinoma, and it promotes cell proliferation through ERK signaling and cyclin D1–dependent G1/S progression [PMID:29420561, PMID:31337972, PMID:30942529, PMID:39841389]. KRT16 directly interacts with APOA1 to promote lipid droplet accumulation, binds 14-3-3σ/ε to restrict type I interferon signaling upstream of RIG-I, and is required in palmoplantar epidermis for subsequent KRT9 expression during site-specific keratinocyte differentiation [PMID:42037661, PMID:30942529].

KRT7 is a type II intermediate filament keratin selectively expressed in simple and transitional epithelia—including lung, cervix, breast, bile duct, renal collecting duct, and bladder urothelium—while absent from gastrointestinal epithelium, hepatocytes, and stratified squamous epithelia [PMID:2436934, PMID:16831889]. In vivo knockout demonstrates that KRT7 maintains bladder urothelial homeostasis by restraining proliferation and supporting expression of its type I assembly partner K18 [PMID:23741325]. In cancer cells, KRT7 promotes migration and epithelial-mesenchymal transition through TGF-β/Smad2/3 and integrin-β1/FAK signaling, and its expression is transcriptionally driven by FoxM1 binding at AP-2 elements in the KRT7 locus, while post-transcriptionally regulated by METTL3-mediated m6A modification of KRT7 mRNA that enhances translational elongation and mRNA stability [PMID:33416175, PMID:32659254, PMID:33795252].

KRTAP4-5 is an ultrahigh-sulfur keratin-associated protein whose mRNA is expressed specifically in the upper cortex of the hair shaft, where it contributes to hair fiber cross-linking and structural integrity [PMID:11279113]. The gene resides within a ~600-kb KAP gene cluster on chromosome 17q12-21 embedded between type I keratin genes, and its allelic diversity is generated by intragenic deletion and duplication of cysteine-rich repeat-encoding sequences [PMID:15955084].

LRRC10B is upregulated upon viral infection and functions as a bridge molecule that facilitates assembly of the ASB8–TBK1/IKKi complex, promoting K48-linked ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of TBK1/IKKi and thereby negatively regulating type I interferon signaling [PMID:32298923]. Independent validation of this bridging role and broader functional characterization are lacking.

MED28 is a dual-compartment scaffolding protein that functions both as a subunit of the Mediator transcriptional co-activator complex and as a cytoplasmic signaling adaptor linking receptor-proximal kinases to downstream proliferative and migratory pathways. Within the nucleus, MED28 operates in the Mediator head module together with Med6, Med8, and Med18 to repress smooth muscle cell differentiation, maintain pluripotency through Oct4/Nanog expression, and regulate cell cycle progression at the G1–S transition and mitosis [PMID:17848560, PMID:26445504, PMID:30970566]. In the cytoplasm, MED28 associates with the actin cytoskeleton and the tumor suppressor merlin (NF2), is phosphorylated at Y64 by Src-family kinases (principally Lck) to create an SH2-binding motif for Grb2, and promotes cell migration and invasion through a MEK1–MMP2 axis and NF-κB–dependent EMT [PMID:15467741, PMID:16899217, PMID:22495818, PMID:27662245]. MED28 also activates Wnt/β-catenin signaling by suppressing the negative regulator HBP1 and promotes AKT/mTOR-dependent proliferation and lipogenesis in cancer cells [PMID:26660958, PMID:38619972].

MINDY1 (FAM63A) is the founding member of the MINDY family of deubiquitinases, distinguished by a structurally unique catalytic domain with a non-canonical Cys-His-Thr active-site triad, an autoinhibitory Cys-loop relieved upon substrate engagement, and exquisite selectivity for K48-linked polyubiquitin chains, which it trims from the distal end using five distinct ubiquitin-binding sites that confer both linkage-type and chain-length sensing [PMID:27292798, PMID:34529927]. By removing K48-linked degradative ubiquitin signals, MINDY1 stabilizes substrates including estrogen receptor α, YAP, and PD-L1, thereby promoting cancer cell proliferation and immune evasion in multiple tumor contexts [PMID:34645792, PMID:34315490, PMID:39217442]. MINDY1 is prenylated, a modification required for its role in embryonic stem cell self-renewal downstream of polyamine signaling [PMID:29644784], and is phosphorylated by AKT at Ser441, functioning as a negative regulator of insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in skeletal muscle [PMID:39577414].

MRPS2 is a structural component of the small (28S) subunit of the mammalian mitochondrial ribosome, homologous to bacterial ribosomal protein S2, and is essential for small subunit assembly, mitochondrial translation, and oxidative phosphorylation [PMID:11279123, PMID:25838379]. Loss of MRPS2 prevents mitoribosomal small subunit biogenesis—demonstrated by complexome profiling—abolishes translation of the 13 mtDNA-encoded OXPHOS subunits, and causes combined deficiency of complexes I and IV, which is rescued by reintroduction of wild-type MRPS2 [PMID:29576219, PMID:40360742]. Bi-allelic loss-of-function mutations in MRPS2 cause combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency presenting in muscle, liver, and skin fibroblasts, validated in patient cells and by zebrafish knockout, establishing MRPS2 as a Mendelian disease gene [PMID:29576219, PMID:40360742].

MRPS28 encodes bS1m, a structural protein of the mitochondrial ribosome small subunit (mtSSU) that is essential for mtSSU assembly, mitochondrial translation, and oxidative phosphorylation. The protein contains a mitochondria-specific N-terminal domain and a C-terminal domain homologous to bacterial ribosomal protein S15; both domains are individually required for assembly into the 28S/37S small subunit, and the N-terminal domain facilitates incorporation of the S15-like domain into the ribosome, as demonstrated by in trans complementation of truncation fragments in yeast [PMID:8411167] and by heterologous rescue of an E. coli S15 mutant [PMID:8411168]. High-resolution cryo-EM of the human mitoribosome places bS1m within the remodeled head domain of the small subunit [PMID:25838379]. Biallelic loss-of-function variants in MRPS28 cause intrauterine growth retardation with craniofacial dysmorphism and multisystemic OXPHOS deficiency, mediated by defective mtSSU assembly and inhibited mitochondrial translation that are rescued by wild-type MRPS28 re-expression [PMID:30566640].

MRPS33 is a mitochondria-specific structural protein of the small (28S) subunit of the mammalian mitochondrial ribosome (mitoribosome), with no homologs in bacterial, chloroplast, archaebacterial, or cytosolic ribosomes [PMID:11279123]. Its position within the 28S subunit was resolved in the 3.5 Å cryo-EM structure of the intact human mitoribosome, confirming its role in the complex that synthesizes the 13 mitochondrially encoded oxidative phosphorylation subunits [PMID:25838379]. Knockout of Mrps33 causes early embryonic lethality in mice, demonstrating non-redundant essentiality among mitoribosomal proteins, and heterozygous disruption of the Drosophila ortholog produces a dosage-sensitive cardiomyopathy phenotype distinct from most other mitoribosomal protein haploinsufficiencies [PMID:32987154, PMID:21890737].

MVD encodes mevalonate diphosphate decarboxylase, which catalyzes the ATP-dependent decarboxylation of mevalonate diphosphate to isopentenyl diphosphate in the mevalonate/isoprenoid biosynthetic pathway, a function conserved from yeast to mammals [PMID:12073030]. MVD physically interacts with mortalin (GRP75), and co-expression of MVD rescues mortalin-induced suppression of Ras and phospho-ERK2 levels, linking MVD to modulation of the Ras-Raf-MAPK proliferation pathway [PMID:12646231]. Biallelic loss-of-function of MVD in keratinocytes—through germline heterozygous mutations combined with somatic second-hit events—drives clonal epidermal expansion causing porokeratosis, while MVD haploinsufficiency in a knock-in mouse model attenuates inflammatory skin responses and activates autophagy [PMID:30942823, PMID:31207227, PMID:37227548].

NDRG3 is a catalytically inactive α/β-hydrolase fold protein that functions as a lactate-responsive signaling scaffold, coupling metabolic state to multiple downstream pathways including Raf-ERK, WNT/β-catenin, and KRAS signaling. Under normoxia, NDRG3 is targeted for proteasomal degradation via PHD2/VHL-mediated ubiquitination, but direct lactate binding during prolonged hypoxia stabilizes the protein, enabling activation of the Raf-ERK pathway to promote angiogenesis and cell growth, and inhibition of ER-to-Golgi trafficking through binding the long isoform of Syntaxin-5 [PMID:25936780, PMID:41252154]. NDRG3 also scaffolds KRAS–USP9X interaction to promote KRAS deubiquitination and stabilization, facilitates β-catenin nuclear translocation downstream of ESR1-driven transcription, fine-tunes HIF-1α signaling by displacing p300, and is itself negatively regulated by SIRT7-dependent deacetylation leading to ubiquitin-proteasomal degradation [PMID:39819877, PMID:31072445, PMID:29760417, PMID:40714033]. Physiologically, tissue-specific knockouts demonstrate essential roles in hepatic glycogen metabolism, male meiotic DNA double-strand break repair via ERK signaling, and naïve CD8+ T cell homeostasis through IL-4/Eomes signaling [PMID:35563842, PMID:28290521, PMID:40073135].

NDUFS1 is the 75 kDa iron-sulfur subunit of mitochondrial complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase) that is essential for electron transfer, complex I assembly, supercomplex stability, and oxidative phosphorylation. Loss-of-function mutations destabilize the N-module, abolish electron transfer between iron-sulfur clusters, and cause complex I deficiency with mitochondrial ROS accumulation, TCA cycle feedback inhibition, and apoptotic pathway activation [PMID:11349233, PMID:31557978, PMID:36462614]. NDUFS1 mitochondrial import requires AKAP1 and is antagonized by MDM2-mediated cytoplasmic sequestration; its activity is further regulated by caspase-3 cleavage at D255 (amplifying apoptotic ROS and lysosomal membrane permeabilization), glutathionylation (promoting reverse-electron-transfer ROS), SIRT3-dependent deacetylation (causing complex I dissociation), and RNF43-mediated ubiquitin-proteasomal degradation [PMID:32072193, PMID:30879903, PMID:23788428, PMID:36290766, PMID:40493314, PMID:38988031]. Biallelic NDUFS1 mutations cause autosomal recessive mitochondrial complex I deficiency [PMID:11349233, PMID:20382551].

NDUFS5 is a small (106-amino acid) accessory subunit of mitochondrial respiratory chain complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase) that contains a Cx(9)C motif and resides in the mitochondrial intermembrane space, where it stabilizes the membrane domain of the complex [PMID:10070614, PMID:21310150]. Import of NDUFS5 into the IMS depends on the AIFM1–MIA40 disulfide relay; when AIFM1 is absent, NDUFS5 accumulates in the cytosol, undergoes proteasomal degradation, and complex I assembly stalls [PMID:35859387]. Incorporation of NDUFS5 into the PP-b module of complex I requires the assembly factors NDUFAF3 and NDUFAF4 [PMID:34386730]. Loss of NDUFS5 disrupts mitochondrial network morphology, and its transcription in spermatogonia is directly controlled by E4F1, linking complex I biogenesis to germ cell maintenance [PMID:40751083, PMID:37749649].

NFE2 (p45 NF-E2) is a hematopoietic-specific CNC-family basic-leucine zipper transcription factor essential for terminal megakaryocyte maturation, proplatelet formation, and erythroid differentiation. It forms obligate heterodimers with small Maf proteins (MafF, MafG, MafK) to bind NF-E2/AP-1-like recognition elements in globin locus control regions and in megakaryocyte-specific gene promoters including thromboxane synthase, β1 tubulin, and Rab27b, with DNA-binding activity augmented by CBP-mediated acetylation of MafG [PMID:8469283, PMID:8107826, PMID:11154691, PMID:9312024, PMID:10942379, PMID:12907454]. NFE2 activity is regulated by competing partners (Bach1, Fos–Maf homodimers) for small Maf binding, by upstream transcriptional activation through AML1/RUNX1, and by an autoregulatory loop involving the histone demethylase JMJD1C that modulates H3K9 methylation at the NFE2 promoter [PMID:8887638, PMID:7891713, PMID:20339092, PMID:29519804]. Overexpression or acquired truncating mutations of NFE2 cause myeloproliferative neoplasms with thrombocytosis and predisposition to leukemic transformation [PMID:22231305, PMID:23589569, PMID:30755419].

NRF1 (also known as NFE2L1 or alpha-Pal/NRF-1) is a CNC-bZIP transcription factor that serves as a master regulator of proteasome homeostasis, antioxidant defense, and mitochondrial biogenesis, coordinating cellular proteostasis with metabolic adaptation. NRF1 is synthesized as an ER-resident glycoprotein anchored by its N-terminal domain; upon proteasome insufficiency it is retrotranslocated to the cytosol, proteolytically cleaved and activated by the aspartyl protease DDI2, deglycosylated by NGLY1, and translocated to the nucleus where it heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins to bind CNC-sMaf-binding elements (CsMBEs) and antioxidant response elements (AREs), driving expression of all 26S proteasome subunit genes, aggrephagy mediators (p62, GABARAPL1), ER homeostasis factors, and cholesterol-elimination genes [PMID:27528193, PMID:27528192, PMID:27676297, PMID:27723178, PMID:35129372, PMID:37658135, PMID:37060561]. NRF1 activity is tuned by O-GlcNAcylation (OGT/HCF-1 complex), non-canonical oxyester-linked ubiquitination (SCF^FBS2–ARIH1), SIAH2-mediated degradation at K230, ATM-dependent phosphorylation promoting nuclear entry under oxidative stress, TBK1 phosphorylation at Ser318 inactivating the NRF1–TFAM axis during viral infection, and HDAC3-mediated deacetylation at K105/K139 [PMID:29941490, PMID:39116872, PMID:30833558, PMID:30642892, PMID:37409632, PMID:39198723]. Beyond proteostasis, NRF1 cooperates with PGC-1α/β and ERRα to activate nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes (TFAM, cytochrome c, FDXR, FUNDC1), is essential for hepatocyte survival and lipid homeostasis, drives spermatogenesis and cardiac regeneration programs, and recruits ncPRC1.3 for neuronal developmental gene activation [PMID:33554448, PMID:26492917, PMID:20561910, PMID:12808106, PMID:25092871, PMID:28754714, PMID:34489413, PMID:34637754].

PHGDH is the rate-limiting NAD⁺-dependent oxidoreductase catalyzing conversion of 3-phosphoglycerate to 3-phosphohydroxypyruvate in de novo serine biosynthesis, thereby coordinating one-carbon metabolism, nucleotide synthesis, redox homeostasis, heme production, and ceramide/lipid metabolism across diverse tissues [PMID:27110680, PMID:30575741, PMID:30017355, PMID:32549981]. Catalytic activity requires homodimerization via the catalytic domain and is positively regulated by PRMT1-mediated arginine methylation (R236, R54, R20) that stabilizes substrate binding and suppresses polyubiquitination, while RNF114-mediated ubiquitination at K310/K330 and Josephin-2-mediated deubiquitination control protein turnover [PMID:33753166, PMID:36823188, PMID:38383964, PMID:35788583, PMID:36583817]. Beyond catalysis, PHGDH functions as a metabolic sensor: when unoccupied by 3-PGA it scaffolds an AXIN–HIPK2 complex that phosphorylates p53-Ser46 to promote apoptosis, it interacts with phosphofructokinase to suppress the hexosamine–sialic acid pathway and metastasis, and upon p38/AMPK-mediated phosphorylation it translocates to the nucleus where its ACT domain binds cMyc to drive chemokine expression and where it oxidizes malate to restrict NAD⁺ availability and PARP1-dependent transcription [PMID:37726403, PMID:35585241, PMID:34663976, PMID:37078828]. These integrated catalytic and non-catalytic roles position PHGDH at the nexus of serine metabolism, immune microenvironment remodeling, and cell-fate decisions in contexts including neuronal NMDA receptor signaling, germinal center B cell activation, and tumor progression [PMID:31548413, PMID:35316216, PMID:36804058].

PIK3R2 encodes p85β, a regulatory subunit of class IA phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) that recruits p110 catalytic subunits to activated receptor tyrosine kinases and phosphotyrosine-containing scaffolds (IRS-1, CD133, EpoR) via its tandem SH2 domains, which recognize pYXXM motifs [PMID:1332046, PMID:8599763, PMID:23569237]. p85β forms obligate heterodimers with p110 through its inter-SH2 (iSH2) domain and tonically inhibits catalytic activity through iSH2–C2 and cSH2–p110β contacts that are relieved by phosphopeptide engagement of its SH2 domains; notably, p85β is a weaker inhibitor of p110 than p85α, and its cSH2 domain exerts an activating rather than inhibiting effect, contributing to its oncogenic potential when overexpressed [PMID:21362552, PMID:19915146, PMID:28915558, PMID:25385636]. Beyond canonical PI3K regulation, p85β possesses PI3K-independent functions including RabGAP activity toward Rab5/Rab4 controlling receptor trafficking and transformation [PMID:18387942], interaction with XBP-1s to promote its nuclear translocation and ER stress resolution [PMID:20348926, PMID:25754093], nuclear translocation to stabilize EZH1/2 via USP7 recruitment thereby enhancing H3K27me3 [PMID:35418124], and regulation of AXL autophagic degradation through TRIM2/optineurin phosphorylation [PMID:32385243]. Gain-of-function germline mutations in PIK3R2, most commonly Gly373Arg, cause megalencephaly–polymicrogyria–polydactyly–hydrocephalus (MPPH) syndrome through hyperactivation of PI3K–AKT signaling during brain development [PMID:22729224].

PMVK is a peroxisomally localized kinase that catalyzes the ATP-dependent phosphorylation of mevalonate 5-phosphate to mevalonate 5-diphosphate, an essential step in the mevalonate/isoprenoid biosynthesis pathway [PMID:8188698, PMID:17180682]. The crystal structure of human PMVK reveals an animal-specific protein fold distinct from bacterial phosphomevalonate kinases, with a correspondingly different structural basis for metabolite-mediated inhibition [PMID:20932952]. Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in PMVK cause porokeratosis through a two-hit mechanism (germline plus somatic loss of the wild-type allele) that leads to keratinocyte apoptosis and abnormal differentiation, while biallelic loss-of-function variants can produce a systemic autoinflammatory phenotype with elevated IL-1β [PMID:26202976, PMID:30942823, PMID:38018277]. In Drosophila, the PMVK ortholog acts through the mevalonate pathway and Rheb/TOR signaling to support neuronal axon regrowth during metamorphosis [PMID:30942823].

PPP1R7 (SDS22) is a leucine-rich repeat protein that serves as a central regulator of protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) biogenesis, stability, and substrate targeting throughout eukaryotes. SDS22 forms a horseshoe-shaped LRR scaffold that binds the α5/α6-helix face of PP1, selectively trapping a metal-deficient (M1-lacking) inactive conformation; together with Inhibitor-3, it assembles a catalytically inert SDS22:PP1:I3 ternary complex that stabilizes nascent PP1 against proteasomal degradation and facilitates M2 metal exchange, and this complex is disassembled by the AAA+ ATPase p97/VCP to liberate active PP1 for holoenzyme formation [PMID:31548429, PMID:38042495, PMID:38918402, PMID:39207734]. SDS22-directed PP1 activity dephosphorylates Aurora B at kinetochores to silence the spindle assembly checkpoint during mitotic progression, dephosphorylates ERM proteins to drive cortical relaxation at anaphase cell poles, and negatively regulates AKT, myosin II, and JNK signaling to maintain epithelial integrity and suppress cell migration [PMID:20921135, PMID:26168397, PMID:30500680, PMID:21399659]. PLK1 phosphorylates SDS22 during mitosis to strengthen its PP1 binding and inhibit Aurora B dephosphorylation, providing a mitotic timing mechanism [PMID:27557660].

PPRC1 is a growth-regulated transcriptional coactivator that functions as a critical regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis, respiratory chain gene expression, and cellular stress responses. Knockdown of PPRC1 severely impairs respiratory chain function, reduces expression of complexes I–IV, diminishes mitochondrial ATP production, and causes proliferation of abnormal mitochondria lacking organized cristae [PMID:19036724]. PPRC1 protein stability is controlled post-translationally through an Akt–GSK-3β signaling axis: GSK-3 phosphorylation of C-terminal serine residues promotes PPRC1 degradation, while mitochondrial stress activates Akt to phospho-inactivate GSK-3β and stabilize PPRC1, acting in concert with c-MYC to reprogram gene expression during apoptosis and premature senescence [PMID:27789709, PMID:23364789]. In vivo, heterozygous Pprc1 knockout mice exhibit elevated energy expenditure and resistance to diet-induced obesity, with haploinsufficiency causing downregulation of PGC-1α and PGC-1β in skeletal muscle, confirming a non-redundant role in systemic energy metabolism [PMID:25994039].

PRLHR (GPR10) is a Gq-coupled GPCR that functions as the principal hypothalamic and hindbrain receptor for prolactin-releasing peptide (PrRP), integrating neuroendocrine signals to restrain food intake, promote energy expenditure, and modulate nociception and cardiovascular tone. GPR10 binds PrRP with sub-nanomolar affinity and signals through intracellular calcium mobilization, ERK, Akt, and CREB phosphorylation, but does not engage cAMP pathways [PMID:11030716, PMID:34445614]. Neuron-restricted expression is enforced by an NRSE element in its promoter that is silenced by NRSF in non-neuronal cells [PMID:12417311]. Loss of GPR10 function—in knockout mice, naturally occurring loss-of-function rat mutants, or rare human variants—causes obesity primarily through decreased energy expenditure rather than hyperphagia, accompanied by dyslipidemia, impaired insulin sensitivity, and altered lipid metabolism, while GPR10 also acts in the NTS to reduce meal size and increase core body temperature and functions as a negative modulator of opioid-mediated analgesia [PMID:14742914, PMID:17904108, PMID:36922513, PMID:16299503, PMID:29796829].

PSMA1 is a structural subunit of the 20S proteasome core particle, occupying one of the seven positions in the outer alpha rings that gate substrate access to the inner proteolytic chamber formed by the beta subunits [PMID:8811196, PMID:19489727]. As an integral component of the 26S proteasome, PSMA1 participates in the degradation of ubiquitinated substrates including those delivered through the ER-associated degradation (ERAD) pathway [PMID:22119785]. PSMA1 expression in hematopoietic malignancy cells is regulated by TRAF6, and its knockdown re-sensitizes bortezomib-resistant MDS/AML cells to proteasome inhibitor–induced apoptosis [PMID:22685174]. The long noncoding RNA MDHDH acts as a scaffold to bridge ubiquitinated MDH2 to PSMA1 at the proteasome, promoting MDH2 degradation and thereby modulating NAD⁺ metabolism and glycolysis in glioblastoma cells [PMID:36527092].

RBX1 (ROC1) is the RING-H2 finger protein that serves as the catalytic subunit of cullin-RING E3 ubiquitin ligase (CRL) complexes, directly recruiting and activating E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes to catalyze polyubiquitin chain formation on a broad range of substrates including IκBα, p27, CDT1, Nrf2, Cyclin E, EXO1, and others, thereby governing cell cycle progression, NF-κB signaling, DNA damage responses, and antioxidant defense [PMID:10213691, PMID:10230406, PMID:21115485, PMID:29358211]. RBX1 binds the C-terminal cullin domain of multiple cullins (CUL1–5) through an intermolecular β-sheet to form a two-subunit catalytic core, with its isolated RING domain sufficient to activate E2 enzymes such as CDC34 and UBC5 for ubiquitin chain assembly [PMID:11961546, PMID:11861641, PMID:10230407]. RBX1 also functions as a NEDD8-E3 ligase that recruits UBC12 to promote cullin neddylation—a modification that markedly enhances CRL ubiquitin ligase activity—and its RING domain is the target of regulatory inputs including inhibition by Glomulin (which occludes the E2-binding surface), arsenite binding, and MAGE-C2 binding, as well as stabilization by USP15-mediated deubiquitination [PMID:12565873, PMID:10921923, PMID:22748924, PMID:29658272, PMID:16005295]. RBX1 is essential for mouse embryonic development, with knockout lethality partially rescued by co-deletion of the CRL substrate p27, and Treg-specific deletion causes fatal inflammatory disease linked to disrupted effector Treg homeostasis [PMID:19325126, PMID:35641500].

SAP30BP functions as both a critical activator–scaffold of the CDK11–cyclin L kinase complex that drives global pre-mRNA splicing and a co-repressor component that promotes histone deacetylation and transcriptional silencing. Within the CDK11 complex, SAP30BP stabilizes cyclins L1/L2 and contacts the CDK11 C-terminal kinase lobe to promote complex assembly and kinase activity, enabling phosphorylation of SF3B1 during spliceosome activation at the B-to-Bact transition; acute degradation of SAP30BP phenocopies CDK11 loss with widespread splicing defects, and a neural alternative exon modulates its interactions with RNA processing factors to control splicing of mini-introns [PMID:38059508, PMID:38065061, PMID:42034640, PMID:41428738]. SAP30BP also interacts with SAP30 within the mSin3A/HDAC co-repressor complex and promotes HDAC-mediated deacetylation of histone H3 lysine 9 and lysine 14 to repress transcription [PMID:15496587, PMID:21221920]. Through HDAC1-dependent repression of MFN2 transcription, SAP30BP modulates mitochondrial dynamics and ferroptosis susceptibility in cardiomyocytes [PMID:40774404].

SEBOX is a paired-like homeodomain transcription factor that functions as a maternally stored gene product essential for early embryonic development. Deposited in oocytes, SEBOX protein is dispensable for oocyte maturation but required for progression beyond the two-cell stage; its knockdown prevents degradation of maternal mRNAs (c-mos, Gbx2, Gdf9), blocks zygotic genome activation (Mt1a, Rpl23, Ube2a, Wee1), and derepresses pluripotency genes SOX2 and NANOG [PMID:18753614, PMID:25679966, PMID:24018616]. SEBOX also regulates other maternal effect genes including Figla, linking it to subcortical maternal complex formation, and its own expression is post-transcriptionally controlled by the miR-125 family [PMID:25679966, PMID:27906131]. In Xenopus, SEBOX acts downstream of Nodal/Activin signaling to repress noncanonical Wnt ligands (wnt5a, wnt5b, wnt11b) and is required for mesoderm and head formation during gastrulation [PMID:26285158].

SEC61G is a membrane-integrated subunit of the heterotrimeric SEC61 translocon complex that is essential for protein translocation across the ER membrane, stabilizes the pore-forming Sec61α subunit through mutual interaction, and coordinates translocation with N-linked glycosylation via direct contact with the oligosaccharyltransferase (OST) complex [PMID:8223425, PMID:7961662, PMID:12860997]. Through its canonical translocon function, SEC61G enables ER import and glycosylation of immune checkpoint ligands (PD-L1, PVR, PD-L2), promoting their surface presentation and tumor immune evasion [PMID:37523556]. SEC61G also mediates ER calcium leakage into the cytosol, activating EGFR–calmodulin and Akt pro-survival signaling; its mRNA is post-transcriptionally regulated by a PARP13–BRCA1 axis that modulates SEC61G abundance upon DNA damage [PMID:40413702, PMID:41052987]. Independent of its translocon role, SEC61G stabilizes the glycolytic enzyme PGAM1 by competitively inhibiting UBE3C-mediated ubiquitination, thereby enhancing glycolysis and promoting brain metastatic colonization [PMID:39990664].

SLBP is the central post-transcriptional regulator of replication-dependent histone mRNAs, coupling histone biogenesis to S-phase progression through roles in 3'-end processing, nuclear export, translation, and mRNA degradation. Its RNA-binding domain is intrinsically disordered and folds upon phosphorylation-dependent binding to the conserved 3' stem-loop of histone mRNAs, where a phosphothreonine in the TPNK motif increases RNA affinity by stabilizing a hydrogen-bonding network and slowing the off-rate, while SLBP binding remodels the pre-mRNA to facilitate U7 snRNP recruitment for endonucleolytic cleavage [PMID:22439849, PMID:25379382, PMID:16982637]. SLBP accompanies processed histone mRNA to the cytoplasm for translation, recruiting the translation activator SLIP1—a MIF4G-domain homodimer that bridges SLBP to eIF3—through a phosphorylation-gated heterodimer assembly mechanism [PMID:23804756, PMID:23286197, PMID:19155325]. SLBP abundance is itself cell-cycle-regulated by at least three ubiquitin ligase systems—CRL4(WDR23) activating ubiquitylation during S phase, SCF–cyclin F targeting SLBP for G2 degradation via a CY motif, and FEM1-family CUL2 ligases mediating degradation in other phases—with Pin1/PP2A promoting SLBP dissociation from histone mRNA and subsequent polyubiquitination at the S/G2 boundary [PMID:27203182, PMID:27773672, PMID:28118078, PMID:22907757]. Haploinsufficiency of SLBP in Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome patient cells causes defective chromatin assembly, delayed S-phase progression, and increased DNA damage sensitivity [PMID:22328085].

SLC25A28 (mitoferrin-2) is a mitochondrial inner membrane iron transporter that mediates high-affinity Fe²⁺ import into the mitochondrial matrix, supplying iron for heme biosynthesis, iron-sulfur cluster (ISC) assembly, and electron transport chain function. SLC25A28 and its erythroid paralog SLC25A37 (mitoferrin-1) are functionally redundant: single knockouts are viable, but combined loss causes lethal ISC depletion, respiratory chain failure, and proliferation arrest, establishing the mitoferrin pair as collectively essential for mitochondrial iron homeostasis [PMID:32518166, PMID:38886830]. SLC25A28 transporter activity is positively regulated by mitochondrially-translocated p53 (promoted by BRD7), and its protein abundance is controlled by PINK1-PARK2-mediated mitophagic degradation; excess SLC25A28 drives mitochondrial iron overload that triggers ferroptosis, HIF1α-dependent metabolic reprogramming, and AIM2 inflammasome activation [PMID:32863216, PMID:30100261]. In microglia, SLC25A28-dependent mitochondrial iron import sustains aerobic glycolysis required for inflammatory activation, and in cancer, SLC25A28 suppresses Complex III subunit UQCRC2 to promote ROS accumulation and ferroptosis [PMID:38085466, PMID:41456814].

SLU7 is a conserved pre-mRNA splicing factor that acts at the second catalytic step of splicing to select the 3' splice site and, in mammalian cells, broadly controls alternative splicing programs that maintain hepatocellular differentiation, genome stability, and epigenetic integrity. In the spliceosome, SLU7 is recruited after PRP16 via its zinc knuckle domain and cooperates with Prp18 to enforce 3' splice site choice when the branchpoint-to-3'SS distance exceeds ~7 nucleotides; it is released together with Prp22 upon mRNA liberation [PMID:1427075, PMID:7664739, PMID:8756413, PMID:12212850]. Beyond core splicing, SLU7 preserves DNMT1 protein stability by facilitating its interaction with HDAC1 and USP7, thereby maintaining DNA methylation [PMID:34331453]; it suppresses R-loop formation and sister chromatid cohesion defects by preventing generation of dominant-negative SRSF3 truncations [PMID:30657957]; and it protects HNF4α1 from oxidative-stress-mediated degradation, stabilizes UPF1 to support nonsense-mediated decay, and participates in a G3BP1–PABPC1–eIF4G1 complex that regulates PI3K mRNA translation [PMID:34170569, PMID:39105183, PMID:38084438]. SLU7 itself is subject to caspase-mediated cleavage during liver damage, providing a mechanism for its downregulation in disease [PMID:39105183].

SNRNP40 is a core subunit of the U5 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (snRNP) that functions within the spliceosome to catalyze pre-mRNA splicing. Initially identified by mass spectrometry of purified spliceosomal particles [PMID:9731529], SNRNP40 was confirmed in the catalytic C complex containing U2, U5, and U6 snRNAs [PMID:11991638] and structurally resolved within the human C* spliceosome by cryo-EM [PMID:28076346]. Hypomorphic loss of SNRNP40 in mice causes widespread intron retention across hundreds of transcripts, disrupting expression of immune-function proteins and producing a syndromic immunodeficiency with impaired lymphoid development and susceptibility to viral infection [PMID:31427773]. Reduced SNRNP40 expression in breast cancer cells promotes metastatic colonization, linking spliceosome integrity to metastatic fitness [PMID:27138336].

SOX4 is an HMG-box transcription factor that functions as a pioneer factor to remodel chromatin and regulate cell fate decisions across diverse developmental and disease contexts, including EMT, immune regulation, endocrine cell differentiation, and thermogenesis. SOX4 directly binds and activates promoters of target genes (EZH2, Cdkn1a, CXCL12, TMEM2, CXCR7, Cald1, ADAMTS4/5, Dicer, WNT2, BMI1) to drive context-dependent transcriptional programs, and can function as a pioneer factor by closing hepatocyte enhancers and opening biliary regulatory sequences to reprogram cell identity [PMID:38409161, PMID:23764001, PMID:27328729]. Its transcriptional output is shaped by post-translational modifications—KAT5-mediated acetylation at K95 activates target promoters while HDAC1 antagonizes this switch [PMID:26291311]—and by co-factor interactions including p53/p300 complex stabilization [PMID:19234109], an EZH2/HDAC3 co-repressor complex [PMID:25644061], and a PPARγ/PRDM16 coactivator complex that drives thermogenic gene expression in beige adipocytes [PMID:36451857]. De novo heterozygous missense variants in the HMG DNA-binding domain that abolish DNA binding and transactivation cause a neurodevelopmental syndrome [PMID:30661772].

STX10 is a trans-Golgi network (TGN)-localized SNARE protein that participates in retrograde membrane trafficking between endosomes and the TGN. It forms a quaternary SNARE complex with STX16, Vti1a, and VAMP3 that operates downstream of Rab9 and the tether GCC185 to mediate mannose 6-phosphate receptor (MPR) retrieval from late endosomes to the TGN; depletion of STX10 causes MPR missorting and hypersecretion of lysosomal enzymes, defining a transport route distinct from the STX6-dependent pathway used for TGN46 and cholera toxin [PMID:18195106]. STX10 interacts with the GARP tethering complex via hVps52, linking vesicle docking to SNARE-mediated fusion at the TGN [PMID:15878329], and also co-immunoprecipitates endosomal syntaxin 12/13; its knockdown alters transferrin receptor surface expression, indicating an additional role at the TGN–endosome boundary [PMID:16154903].

TBL3 is a conserved WD-40 repeat protein that functions as an essential subunit of the UTP-B sub-complex within the 90S pre-ribosomal SSU processome, where it is required for early pre-rRNA processing cleavages (A0, A1, A2) and correct 5'ETS removal during 40S ribosomal subunit biogenesis [PMID:15231838, PMID:39036955]. TBL3 localizes to the dense fibrillar component of the nucleolus with very low mobility indicative of tight macromolecular complex association, and its position within the processome places it in direct proximity to the 5' end of nascent pre-rRNA [PMID:24754225, PMID:35076539]. In vertebrates, TBL3 loss of function slows cell cycle progression in a p53-independent, tissue-specific manner affecting hematopoietic, retinal, and other progenitor cell populations [PMID:22659140]. TBL3 also directly contacts mRNA in living cells and can be aberrantly sequestered by expanded CAG-repeat transcripts, correlating with disrupted rRNA processing in Huntington's disease and SCA2 brain tissue [PMID:22658674, PMID:34390268].

TMED2 is a p24-family type I transmembrane cargo sorting adaptor that cycles between the ER, ER-Golgi intermediate compartment, and cis-Golgi to control the biosynthetic trafficking, ER retention, and plasma membrane delivery of diverse transmembrane client proteins. Its luminal GOLD domain directly binds GPCRs (PAR-1, PAR-2, P2Y receptors, µ-opioid receptor), Smoothened, TLRs (TLR2/3/4), calcium-sensing receptor, and fibronectin, retaining them in early secretory compartments until regulated release — for example, ARF1-dependent dissociation triggers PAR-2 forward transport, while TMED2 loss allows uncontrolled SMO accumulation at the plasma membrane and ectopic Hedgehog signaling [PMID:17693410, PMID:35353806, PMID:37491993]. Together with TMED10, TMED2 forms a supercomplex at ER–Golgi membrane contact sites that mediates cholesterol and ceramide exchange, thereby shaping plasma membrane lipid nanodomains required for toxin oligomerization and signaling platform assembly [PMID:36174556]. Upon DNA virus infection, TMED2 associates with STING/MITA in a stimulus-dependent manner, reinforcing STING dimerization and ER-to-perinuclear vesicle trafficking to potentiate type I interferon production [PMID:30540941].

TOMM22 is the central organizer and presequence receptor of the mitochondrial translocase of the outer membrane (TOM) complex, coordinating precursor protein recognition, channel gating, and higher-order complex assembly. Its cytosolic domain—a three-helix bundle structurally similar to Tom20—binds presequence-carrying precursors and hands them to the IMS domain, which transfers them to Tim50 of the TIM23 inner-membrane translocase, establishing a relay across the outer membrane [PMID:21896724, PMID:35733257, PMID:9252394]. Phosphorylation by CK2 (Ser44/Ser46) promotes Tom22 import and controls PINK1-dependent mitophagy in skeletal muscle, CK1 (Thr57) stimulates its assembly with Tom20, and PKA (Thr76) opposes import, while porin/VDAC acts as a chaperone sink regulating Tom22 integration into the trimeric TOM complex [PMID:24093680, PMID:29165030, PMID:30738703]. Beyond protein import, TOMM22 serves as the mitochondrial receptor for pro-apoptotic Bax—recognizing its GALLL motif and stimulating C-terminal helix membrane insertion—and participates in steroidogenic complexes with 3βHSD2 and aldosterone synthase [PMID:17096026, PMID:39043635, PMID:26787839].

TOPBP1 is a multi-BRCT-domain scaffold protein that serves as the principal activator of ATR checkpoint kinase signaling and an essential platform for DNA replication initiation, DNA repair, and mitotic genome stability. Its intrinsically disordered ATR-activation domain (AAD) directly stimulates ATR-ATRIP kinase activity, and this activation is amplified by liquid-liquid phase separation of TOPBP1 into condensates; AAD function is essential for viability, as a W1147R knock-in is embryonic lethal in mice [PMID:16530042, PMID:33503405, PMID:23950734]. TOPBP1 is recruited to damaged or stalled replication forks through phospho-dependent interactions mediated by its tandem BRCT domains—BRCT1-2 binds CK2-phosphorylated Rad9 (9-1-1 clamp), BRCT4-5 binds 53BP1 for the G1 checkpoint, and BRCT7-8 binds BACH1/FANCJ—while CDK-phosphorylated Treslin/TICRR engages BRCT3-4 to trigger replication origin firing [PMID:26724438, PMID:30295604, PMID:20116089, PMID:31135337]. Beyond checkpoint and replication roles, Akt phosphorylation at Ser-1159 drives TOPBP1 oligomerization via BRCT7-8, switching its function from ATR activation to E2F1 transcriptional repression, and during mitosis TOPBP1 forms CIP2A–MDC1-dependent filamentous structures that tether DSBs to prevent chromosome mis-segregation [PMID:24081328, PMID:30898438, PMID:35842428].

TRIM24 is a multifunctional chromatin reader and RING-domain E3 ubiquitin ligase that integrates histone mark recognition with transcriptional co-activation and targeted protein degradation. Its tandem PHD-bromodomain reads a combinatorial histone signature—unmethylated H3K4 and acetylated H3K23—on the same histone tail, directing chromatin binding that is coupled to co-activation of nuclear receptors (ER, AR, RARα) and transcription factors (STAT3) at target gene promoters, and to restriction of p53 activity at closed chromatin loci [PMID:21164480, PMID:37386214, PMID:29129908, PMID:27238081]. Through its RING domain, TRIM24 ubiquitinates p53 for proteasomal degradation in a pathway regulated by ATM phosphorylation and a p53-driven transcriptional feedback loop, catalyzes K63-linked ubiquitination of TRAF3 to activate antiviral type I interferon signaling, and ubiquitinates CBP to promote Stat6 acetylation during macrophage polarization [PMID:19556538, PMID:24820418, PMID:32324863, PMID:31554795]. TRIM24 protein stability is itself controlled by SPOP-mediated ubiquitination counteracted by TRIM28 binding, and Akt-mediated phosphorylation triggers its nuclear-to-cytoplasmic translocation, where it regulates P-body-dependent mRNA stability [PMID:30479348, PMID:27238081, PMID:35803934].

TTC31 is a tetratricopeptide repeat-containing protein whose molecular function remains uncharacterized. Its gene is transcribed from a bidirectional, TATA-less CpG-island-associated promoter shared with CCDC142 at chromosomal locus 2p13.1, containing Inr, BRE, and DPE elements [PMID:21790010].

Urocortin (UCN) is a corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF)-family neuropeptide that functions as a high-affinity ligand for both CRF receptor type 1 (CRF1R) and type 2 (CRF2R), coupling to Gs-mediated cAMP signaling and ACTH secretion [PMID:8612563]. Cryo-EM structures show UCN1 adopts a single straight α-helix whose N-terminus inserts into the receptor transmembrane bundle, with distinct contact residues governing differential CRF1R versus CRF2R binding specificity [PMID:32004470, PMID:24290358]. UCN is produced in multiple peripheral tissues including cardiomyocytes, mast cells, and lymphocytes, where it signals cardioprotection through p42/44 MAPK and Akt pathways and promotes chondrocyte survival by CRF1R-cAMP-mediated inactivation of PLA2, preventing Piezo1-dependent calcium influx and apoptosis [PMID:14519439, PMID:28698554, PMID:11788672, PMID:9467598]. UCN gene transcription is regulated by a CRE-containing promoter responsive to cAMP, and the CRF-binding protein modulates UCN bioavailability by sequestering the peptide [PMID:9628819, PMID:8612563].

VWA1 encodes WARP, a secreted, disulfide-bonded multimeric extracellular matrix glycoprotein that stabilizes basement membrane and pericellular matrix architecture in peripheral nerves, cartilage, and muscle by bridging perlecan and collagen VI [PMID:16407285, PMID:23300779]. WARP binds perlecan domain III-2 and heparan sulfate chains with low-nanomolar affinity and associates with the triple-helical domain of collagen VI (KD ~22 nM); loss of WARP in mice causes severe mislocalization of collagen VI microfibrils in peripheral nerves, Schwann cell basement membrane fusion, and peripheral neuropathy [PMID:19279005, PMID:23300779]. Bi-allelic loss-of-function variants in VWA1, including a founder 10-bp repeat expansion, cause autosomal-recessive hereditary motor neuropathy and neuromyopathy in humans [PMID:33559681, PMID:33459760]. In cranial neural crest cells, VWA1 promotes osteogenic differentiation through a KDM6B–H3K27me3–Runx2 epigenetic axis and modulates chondrocyte mechanotransduction via FGF9/FGFR3 signaling [PMID:41196123, PMID:40450276].

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific C2H2 zinc-finger transcription factor that activates transcription from both RNA polymerase II and III promoters, with critical roles in mitochondrial gene expression, ribosomal gene regulation, and cell-cycle control. It binds a conserved SBS motif at over 900 mammalian promoters using zinc fingers 1–6 in a target-dependent manner, possesses two separable N-terminal activation domains for mRNA and snRNA promoters, and forms a chromatin-bound complex with THAP11 and HCFC1 to regulate cell-cycle genes [PMID:9566884, PMID:25437553, PMID:17092945]. Acute protein degradation studies demonstrated that ZNF143 functions principally as an essential transcriptional regulator—activating nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes and facilitating RNA polymerase II initiation at most targets while directly repressing a subset of genes by occluding transcription initiation sites—rather than as a general chromatin looping factor, with earlier looping associations partly attributable to antibody cross-reactivity with CTCF [PMID:39708803, PMID:39708805, PMID:39676670]. Loss-of-function mutations in ZNF143 cause an inborn error of cobalamin metabolism linked to reduced MMACHC expression [PMID:27349184].

ZNF284 is a KRAB-domain-containing zinc finger protein encoded within a primate-expanded tandem gene cluster on chromosome 19q13, consistent with a role as a transcriptional repressor [PMID:12743021]. It lacks a clear mouse ortholog, indicating lineage-specific acquisition during primate evolution [PMID:12743021]. Beyond detection in large-scale human protein interactome maps, no direct functional or mechanistic experiments defining its molecular targets, DNA-binding specificity, or biological roles have been reported [PMID:28514442, PMID:33961781].

cluster_genes.UniProt_functional_annotation: May be involved in transcriptional regulation

cluster_genes.affinage_functional_annotation: ZRANB2 is a nuclear RNA-binding protein that functions as a regulator of alternative pre-mRNA splicing through direct recognition of AGGUAA motifs via its two RanBP2-type C4 zinc finger domains. The zinc fingers adopt zinc-ribbon folds in which zinc coordination is essential for structural integrity and high-affinity single-stranded RNA binding; the two domains cooperate to engage tandem AGGUAA sites in pre-mRNA substrates such as TRA2B, DRD2, and ECT2, and their RNA-binding activity is abolished by arsenite-mediated zinc displacement or by persulfidation of the cysteine ligands [PMID:19304800, PMID:32274925, PMID:41558086]. An RS domain mediates nuclear speckle localization and protein–protein interactions with spliceosomal components U1-70K, U2AF35, and XE7/SFRS17A, and ZRANB2 resides within the supraspliceosome, consistent with its role in controlling exon inclusion across diverse transcripts [PMID:11448987, PMID:23666063]. Beyond splicing, ZRANB2 interacts with Smad1/5/8 through its glutamine-rich domain and suppresses BMP-dependent transcription without affecting Smad phosphorylation or nuclear entry, as demonstrated in mammalian cells and zebrafish embryos [PMID:22021003].
